lead: Embedded C is C used to control hardware directly. It keeps C syntax and relies on the standard fixed-width types from the stdint.h header, together with volatile register accesses, bit masks and interrupt functions. A register is a small hardware location; memory-mapped I/O places it at a fixed address. You read or write it through a pointer. This matters in every microcontroller: setting a GPIO pin, clearing a flag, starting an ADC, or handling a timer interrupt. Some syllabi call this C programming for 8051 or ARM. Hosted C on a laptop hides hardware; embedded C exposes it.
prereq: You need: Unit 2 for 8051 and ARM registers; Unit 3 for GPIO and interrupts.

blocks.text: Standard C types like int can change width between compilers. Embedded C uses <stdint.h>: uint8_t is an unsigned 8-bit integer, int16_t is signed 16-bit, uint32_t is unsigned 32-bit. The width is fixed, so register layouts stay correct.

A hardware register is a memory word wired to a peripheral. Memory-mapped I/O gives it an address. In C, cast that address to a pointer and dereference: volatile uint8_t *p = (volatile uint8_t *)0x40000000;. Here p holds the register address, *p is the byte in the register.

volatile tells the compiler the value may change outside normal code, so every read and write must reach memory. Without volatile, an optimiser can cache a status flag in a register and loop forever. const says your code will not write the object; volatile const uint32_t *status is common for read-only status registers.
Hosted C assumes an operating system, files and printf. Embedded C often has no OS, a small standard library, and a startup file. It talks to addresses, not devices.

sections.h3: Bit masks and special function registers

blocks.text: A bit mask is a number with 1s only where you want action. For bit n, (1 << n) has a single 1 at position n and 0 everywhere else. Bit numbering is usually 0 for least significant bit (LSB).
PORT |= (1 << n); PORT &= ~(1 << n); PORT ^= (1 << n); test = (PORT >> n) & 1;
blocks.where: PORT is the register byte; n is the bit number, 0 for LSB; << shifts left; ~ flips all bits; |, &, ^ are bitwise OR, AND, XOR; test is 0 or 1.

blocks.text: In 8051 C, special function registers (SFRs) are accessed with compiler keywords: sfr P1 = 0x90; sbit LED = P1^3; P1 is the port register at SFR address 0x90; LED names bit 3. In ARM C, use a volatile pointer to the GPIO register. Writing the whole byte, as in P1 |= 0x08, is a read-modify-write: read the byte, change bits, write back. Writing one sbit, as in LED = 1, uses an atomic bit instruction such as SETB or CLR, not a byte read-modify-write. On ARM the pointer write is a read-modify-write of the register.

An interrupt service routine (ISR) is a function the hardware calls when an event occurs. In C it is marked with a compiler extension, such as __interrupt or __attribute__((interrupt)). The ISR must be short: set a flag, copy a byte, clear the interrupt source. It must not call printf or block.

Reentrancy means a function can be called again before an earlier call finishes. An ISR and main can share a variable; mark it volatile. If a 16-bit variable is changed in main and read in an ISR on an 8-bit CPU, the read can see half-updated bytes. Disable interrupts around the access or use an atomic type.

Startup code runs before main. It sets the stack pointer, copies initialised data from flash to RAM, clears zeroed data, and calls main. Inline assembly uses __asm volatile ("nop"); for exact instructions. Compiler extensions add SFR names, interrupt vectors and pragmas. The cross-compiler and linker are covered in 6.2.

figure.caption: Cells run from bit 0 on the left to bit 7 on the right. Bit 3 is set with OR mask 0x08 and bit 5 is cleared with AND mask 0xDF; the final byte is 0x8D.

spec.title: Port bit masking
spec.aria: The cells run from bit 0 on the left to bit 7 on the right. An 8-bit port register 0xA5 (1010 0101) is ORed with 0x08 to set bit 3, then ANDed with 0xDF to clear bit 5, giving 0x8D (1000 1101).

examples.question: PORT1 holds 0xA5. Write C using a volatile pointer to set bit 3 and then clear bit 5. Give the two mask values and the final byte.
steps: 0xA5 in binary is 1010 0101. Bit 3 is the fourth bit from the right, value 0x08.
examples.answer: Set mask is 0x08 (8), clear mask is 0xDF (223), and the final byte is 0x8D (141).
examples.check:
a = 0xA5
set_mask = 1 << 3
after = a | set_mask
clear_mask = ~(1 << 5) & 0xFF
final = after & clear_mask
print(a)
print(set_mask)
print(after)
print(clear_mask)
print(final)

traps: Forgetting volatile on a memory-mapped register: the optimiser may keep the old value in a CPU register.
*p |= 0x08 & 0x20 is wrong for two masks: bitwise AND binds before OR, so 0x08 & 0x20 is 0. Use *p |= (0x08 | 0x20).
Using = instead of |= or &= in a read-modify-write line: = overwrites the whole port.
Assuming bit 0 is the leftmost bit in a diagram: standard C numbering starts at the least significant bit.
Treating a 16-bit read-modify-write as atomic on an 8-bit CPU: an interrupt between byte accesses can corrupt the value.

quiz.q: What does volatile tell the compiler?
quiz.a: The object may change outside normal program flow, so every access must read or write memory.

quiz.q: Why use uint8_t instead of int for an 8-bit register?
quiz.a: uint8_t has exactly 8 bits on every compiler; int may be 16 or 32 bits, so it can change register access width.

quiz.q: PORT1 = 0x3C. Write C to set bit 0 and clear bit 2. Give the masks and final byte.
quiz.a: Set mask 1 << 0 = 0x01: 0x3C | 0x01 = 0x3D. Clear mask ~(1 << 2) & 0xFF = 0xFB: 0x3D & 0xFB = 0x39. Final byte 0x39.

quiz.q: An ISR increments a 16-bit counter; main reads it on an 8-bit CPU. Why can the read be wrong? Give one fix.
quiz.a: The 16-bit read takes two byte reads. An interrupt between them can change the high byte after the low byte was read. Fix: disable interrupts around the read, or use an atomic 16-bit access.

quiz.q: Name two stdint types and their widths.
quiz.a: uint8_t is unsigned 8-bit; int16_t is signed 16-bit.

quiz.q: Why is *p |= 0x08 & 0x20 wrong for setting bits 3 and 5?
quiz.a: Bitwise AND has higher precedence than OR. 0x08 & 0x20 is 0, so *p is ORed with 0 and no bit is set. Write *p |= (0x08 | 0x20) for the two bits.

quiz.q: Write one C line using volatile pointer p to toggle bit 4 of a port.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry uses MISRA C rules, static analysers, and hardware abstraction layers to keep register code safe. Rust and C++ are gaining ground for embedded work, but C remains the register-level language. Search terms: MISRA C, volatile pointer, memory-mapped I/O, linker script, startup code.
